Ecommerce website design

Ecommerce websites for local businesses that sell products

Online stores for local businesses that sell products, built for Denton and DFW.

What this is

Selling online as a local business is a different problem from selling nationally. You are usually competing on being nearby and being trusted rather than on price, and a lot of your orders will be picked up rather than shipped.

That changes the build. The store has to handle local pickup as a first-class option, not a checkbox buried at checkout.

What you get

What a store needs

  • 01

    Product pages that answer questions

    Real photographs, sizes, materials, what is in stock, and what happens if it is wrong. Most abandoned carts are unanswered questions rather than price objections.

  • 02

    A short checkout

    Every extra step loses orders. Guest checkout, sensible defaults, and no account creation demanded before someone can give you money.

  • 03

    Local pickup and delivery

    Set up properly, with the pickup location and timing clear before checkout rather than discovered afterwards. For a lot of local sellers this is most of the volume.

  • 04

    Shipping that is not a surprise

    Rates visible early. Shipping revealed at the last step is the single most common reason a cart gets abandoned.

  • 05

    Product structured data

    So search engines can read price and availability rather than guessing at them. Covered in more depth under schema markup.

What it costs

Quoted after a free consult, because what it takes depends entirely on what you already have. Book a call, I will tell you what is involved, and you get a number before anything starts. If you are already on a plan, this may fold into it: the tiers are on the pricing page.

Stores are quoted individually. The size of the catalogue, whether you need stock tracking, and how you handle fulfilment move the number more than the page count does.

How this differs

A normal website design build is aimed at producing a phone call or a quote request. Here the transaction completes on the site, which changes almost everything downstream: payments, stock, tax, shipping, refunds, and what happens when an order goes wrong.

That difference is why this is a separate service rather than a bigger version of the same one.

If you sell a handful of items occasionally, a full store may be more machinery than you need, and a simpler page with a way to order might serve you better. I will say so on the consult rather than sell you the bigger thing.

Questions

What people ask

What platform do you build on?

That is decided on the consult, based on what you sell and how you fulfil. Committing to a platform before understanding the business is how people end up paying monthly for capability they never use.

Who handles payments?

Payments run through an established payment provider, so card details never touch your site. You hold the account and the money goes to you directly.

Can I add products myself?

That is usually the intention, and it is worth saying up front if it matters, because it affects how the store is set up.

Is there a catalogue size where this stops being a fit?

Yes. A few hundred products with variants and stock tracking is a different class of project from twenty. Tell me roughly how many and I will be straight about whether I am the right person.

Sell to the people already nearby

Tell me what is going on and I will tell you whether this is what you actually need. No pitch deck and no pressure.
